title: What a null result actually tells you
text:
The FAMOUS trial asked whether case-based care of multimorbid patients by advanced practice nurses, working inside general practices, would reduce ambulatory emergency contacts over twelve months. It was a two-arm, non-randomised, multicentre interventional study, funded by the German Innovationsfonds, with 2,451 patients enrolled — well above the recruitment target.
The answer was no. Neither the primary endpoint nor any secondary endpoint showed a reduction against routine care.
I was the study statistician for the quantitative evaluation: I wrote the statistical analysis plan and ran every endpoint analysis. So this is the result I had to write up, and the temptation in that position is real. There is always a subgroup that looks better, always a sensitivity analysis that could be promoted to the headline. Resisting that is most of the job.

title: What a null result actually tells you
text:
Why the analysis moved
The protocol had planned a t-test and Poisson regression. The observed data had neither the distribution nor the dispersion for it: excess zeros, because most patients have no emergency contact at all in a year, and overdispersion among those who do.
So the primary analysis moved to a Bayesian zero-inflated negative binomial model with weakly-informative priors, fitted by MCMC in brms/Stan, reporting incidence rate ratios with credible intervals. Control patients were matched 1:2 on age, sex, and the number and type of chronic conditions.
That is a deviation from the protocol, and the right way to handle a deviation is to document it and its rationale rather than to quietly perform it. It went into the evaluation report with the reasoning attached.

title: What a null result actually tells you
section: Why the result was probably null
text:
Why the result was probably null
A null result is only useful if you are honest about which of the plausible explanations you cannot rule out. Four mattered here.
The design was not randomised. Practices opted in, and patients in participating practices differ from those who are not. Matching on age, sex and chronic-condition count narrows the gap; it does not close it.
Routine claims data capture severity poorly. Statutory health-insurance records are excellent at telling you that a contact happened and almost silent on how ill the person was. Much of what an advanced practice nurse might plausibly change is invisible in that data.
The baseline assumption was too high. Power was calculated against an expected 2.7 emergency contacts per person-year, a figure drawn from nursing-home literature. The population actually enrolled was not that population, and the real rate was lower — which makes a given absolute reduction much harder to detect.
COVID-19 was not modelled. The study ran across a period when patterns of ambulatory care contact changed for reasons that had nothing to do with the intervention.

title: What a null result actually tells you
text:
The part worth keeping
The most useful sentence in a null trial report is usually the one that says which assumption was wrong, because that is the sentence the next study needs. Here it was the baseline event rate: an effect size justified from a literature about a different population.
Reporting that plainly costs nothing except the pleasant story. It is also the only version of the result that anyone can build on.

I am a biostatistician based in Mainz, Germany. For six years I worked at the Institute of Medical Biostatistics, Epidemiology and Informatics (IMBEI), Universitätsmedizin Mainz, on oncology biostatistics and investigator-initiated clinical trials, alongside health-services research.
My methodological focus is applied Bayesian modelling and design — Bayesian compartment modelling of MRI time-series, Bayesian additive regression trees on high-dimensional omics, precision-based sample-size determination, and a Bayesian zero-inflated negative binomial primary trial analysis.
I am completing a PhD in the Faculty of Biology at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz on omics-based biomarker discovery for familial pancreatic cancer using machine learning.

title: Chung Shing Rex Ha
text:
What I do
Clinical trial statistics. Statistical analysis plans on the ICH E9(R1) estimand framework, sample-size and power calculations, primary-endpoint analysis, and the statistical sections of ethics-committee and funder submissions.
Machine learning on omics data. Model-based gradient boosting with stability selection, Bayesian additive regression trees and Gaussian graphical models applied to high-dimensional proteomics and LC-MS metabolomics, with explainable-ML methods to make model behaviour interpretable to clinical collaborators.
Statistical consulting. Six years advising doctoral candidates and research groups across more than fifteen clinical departments — translating clinical questions into designs, endpoints and analysis plans, and delivering publication-ready results.
